section: 5 Getis–Ord Gi*: hot and cold spots
text:
5 Getis–Ord Gi*: hot and cold spots
Gi* tests whether high or low values in a neighbourhood as a whole are unusually concentrated. It differs from local Moran’s I: the focal county is included in the Gi* neighbourhood, and the output describes a hot or cold concentration rather than a high/low quadrant pairing. Here I choose the minimum distance that connects the county network, about 60.8 km, then include the focal county. This threshold is calculated on EPSG:32650 metre coordinates. Its neighbourhood sizes range from 2 to 7, including self. I also try six nearest neighbours plus self as a sensitivity check.


Show R code
threshold_m <- sfdep::critical_threshold(sf::st_geometry(hunan_m))
fixed_nb <- sfdep::include_self(sfdep::st_dist_band(
  sf::st_geometry(hunan_m), upper = threshold_m + 1))
fixed_wt <- sfdep::st_weights(fixed_nb, style = "W")
set.seed(62654)
gi <- sfdep::local_gstar_perm(hunan_m$GDPPC, fixed_nb, fixed_wt,
                              alternative = "two.sided", nsim = 999)
gi$p_bh <- p.adjust(gi$p_sim, method = "BH")

7 What I learned
Global significance does not automatically translate into strong evidence for individual counties. A single GDP per capita map shows where county values were high at one point in time. It misses how the spatial concentration of high and low values changes. The package output includes 44 counties with an unadjusted Mann–Kendall trend p <= 0.05, and 43 after BH adjustment across locations. The maps group detailed package labels into hot-spot and cold-spot families for legibility; the table and CSV retain their exact classifications. Grey means the trend test did not pass the indicated threshold, not that GDPPC is zero or that the county has no temporal change.

7.1 A methodological distinction
The class overview describes FDR correction as part of the general EHSA approach. In the installed sfdep implementation, the classification is based on simulated Gi* p-values at its threshold; the function does not itself apply an FDR adjustment to every space-time bin. I separately apply BH within each annual spatial-only Gi* slice and across the 88 county trend tests, and label those checks clearly. This page therefore does not claim exact equivalence with Esri’s FDR-corrected EHSA procedure. The annual spatial-only and lagged EHSA analyses also have different temporal neighbourhoods and simulation counts.

text:
8 What I learned
The biggest practical lesson was about row order: a valid-looking map can be wrong if time-series rows and polygon neighbours are paired by position without a key check. I also learned to ask which Gi* series a trend test is describing. Changsha’s spatial-only trend is positive, while the EHSA classification uses a time-lagged neighbourhood and tells a different, categorical story. Finally, the difference between unadjusted and BH-filtered maps showed me how much caution is needed when looking at many counties over many years. The teaching extract uses one boundary layer for the full period, does not document boundary changes or a price deflator, and cannot support causal claims about regional policy or living standards.

title: Myanmar’s changing conflict geography
text:
Research question: Where is recorded armed conflict concentrated in Myanmar, and which township neighbourhoods are becoming more concentrated over time?
The analysis covers 53,899 events and 89,005 reported fatalities, from January 2021 to September 2025. It combines local spatial statistics with 19 quarterly observations. A spatial scan then asks where conflict gained a larger share of the national total.
Executive summary · GitHub project

title: Myanmar’s changing conflict geography
text:
1 Study context and design
Conflict monitoring has to answer two different planning questions. A township with a large accumulated burden may need sustained humanitarian support. A township where the surrounding concentration is increasing may need closer monitoring even if its historical total is smaller. This report keeps those signals separate.
The study follows the Take-home Exercise 2 brief. The geographical unit is the township, using MIMU v9.4, and the observation period is 1 January 2021–30 September 2025. The brief’s two references to passenger trips and hexagons are treated as editing errors because its objectives and data specification require Myanmar conflict events and townships.
I use three ACLED event types: Battles, Explosions/Remote violence, and Violence against civilians. This operational definition focuses on armed conflict. It excludes riots, protests and strategic developments, including some events that ACLED classifies under its wider definition of political violence. One coded event is the unit of observation. Several events can share a date and location without being duplicates. Reported fatalities are an additional burden measure, with uncertainty in reporting and estimation.
The questions are:

Which townships form high or low clusters, and which contrast with their neighbours?
Which neighbourhood concentrations intensify, diminish or appear intermittently?
Where did the share of national recorded conflict increase between comparable early and recent windows?

Counts measure the geography of reported conflict activity. They do not estimate the probability that an individual experiences harm. No reliable, time-matched population or exposure denominator is supplied.

title: Myanmar’s changing conflict geography
text:
2 Data preparation and quality assessment

2.1 Sources and input checks
The original eLearn ACLED CSV contains 87,109 rows and 31 columns. Its dates cover the full study window. No exact duplicate rows or repeated event IDs were found, and dates, coordinates and fatalities have no missing values. Other fields do contain missing entries, so removing every row with any missing field would discard usable events.
The source contains six records labelled Indian Ocean, which are excluded by the Myanmar country filter. The latest record-update timestamp is 29 September 2026, 22:19:21 UTC. That field describes a record update, not a documented export date. I accessed the supplied course file on 8 October 2026 and pin its SHA-256 hash for replication.
MIMU’s GeoNode layer contains 330 polygons, all labelled P-code version 9.4. Township P-codes are complete and unique. The original WGS84 geometries are valid. st_transform() puts the polygons and event points in a Myanmar-centred Albers equal-area projection, avoiding reliance on a single UTM zone across the country. st_make_valid() is a defensive step and does not repair any invalid input polygons in this snapshot.

4 Local measures of spatial association

4.1 What the tests assess
Global Moran’s I supplies a broad check: I = 0.488, with permutation p = 0.001. The alternative is positive autocorrelation. The 999 permutations randomly reassign event totals over the fixed township graph. This supports examining local concentrations, but it does not identify their causes.
Local Moran’s I compares a township’s deviation from the mean with its neighbours’ average deviation. Row-standardised Queen weights exclude the township itself. High-high and low-low are clusters; high-low and low-high are spatial outliers. localmoran_perm() holds the focal value fixed and permutes neighbour values, without repeated draws within a simulated neighbourhood. Quadrants use the mean-centred variable and its spatial lag, not the sign of I alone.
Getis–Ord Gi* asks whether a neighbourhood sum is unusually high or low. Its weights include the focal township. localG_perm() provides conditional permutation inference. I use the alternative-aware two-sided simulated p-value, rather than the folded tail probability. All primary LMSA colours require p < .05. Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) adjusted values are retained to show the effect of testing many townships. These are exploratory tests of spatially exchangeable values, not a model of population exposure or conflict mechanisms.

Reported fatalities give a different classification because severity and event frequency do not rank every township identically. 5 Emerging hot spot analysis

5.1 Space-time Gi* and Mann–Kendall
spacetime() constructs the quarterly cube and checks its balance. I then explicitly build each bin’s neighbourhood from the township and its Queen neighbours in the current and immediately preceding quarter (k = 1). The combined space-time weights sum to one. The first quarter has no earlier quarter and therefore a shorter temporal neighbourhood. Its results are an endpoint-sensitive baseline.
spdep::localG_perm() computes Gi* on this explicit graph. Standardisation uses the mean and variance across all 6,213 mainland township-quarter bins, and conditional permutations hold the focal bin fixed while reassigning other bin values across that space-time reference. I use its alternative-aware two-sided simulated p-value, not its folded tail probability. This differs from sfdep 0.2.5’s classroom routine, which combines quarter-specific standardisation with permutations pooled across periods. A fixed reference makes the interpretation here explicit: high or low concentration relative to the complete observed space-time distribution. National changes in event frequency can therefore contribute to temporal trends. The redistribution scan later conditions on national window totals to address that separate issue.
Mann–Kendall tests the ordered series of space-time Gi* at each township. Positive tau means increasing concentration against this fixed reference; it is not a rate of change in event counts.
Classification rules are explicit in methods.R: a new class has only its final bin significant in that family; a consecutive class has a final uninterrupted run; intensifying, persistent and diminishing classes require at least 90% of bins in the same family. The trend direction separates intensification from diminution. Sporadic and oscillating classes require a significant final bin; oscillating locations have also experienced the opposite family. Historical classes have at least 90% qualifying earlier bins and a final bin outside that family. These are transparent R adaptations of the Esri pattern definitions, not a claim to reproduce ArcGIS’s complete FDR implementation.


5.2 Patterns with significant temporal evidence






Figure 5: Emerging hot spot classes filtered by significant Mann Kendall trends




165 of 327 townships have ordinary Mann–Kendall p < .05; 150 remain after BH adjustment across township trend tests. The map shows classified patterns only where the trend has p < .05. This meets the brief’s significance filter but deliberately omits persistent locations without a significant trend. Their classes remain in the table and downloadable results. Increasing Gi* indicates a rising neighbourhood concentration against the fixed space-time reference. It can reflect national escalation as well as a geographical change, which motivates the separate redistribution scan.

Of the significant trends, 85 also satisfy an EHSA class. A trend alone does not guarantee a hot- or cold-spot pattern under the final-bin and persistence rules.

Consecutive hot spots. Fourteen townships in this class also have significant MK trends. The largest event totals include Madaya in Mandalay, Nawnghkio in northern Shan, and Yesagyo in Magway. Sporadic hot spots. Twelve locations have significant trends, including Kawkareik and Myawaddy in Kayin and Kyaukkyi in eastern Bago. They end as hot spots after an intermittent history, without a significant cold-spot episode. This eastern and southeastern concentration suggests recurring pressure that a cumulative map alone cannot distinguish from continuous concentration. Kawkareik’s history below helps show the difference.


Oscillating hot spots. Seven locations combine a significant trend with a final hot bin and an earlier cold episode. 5.4 How robust are the patterns?






Figure 7: Emerging hot spot maps under alternative neighbourhood and precision choices




Queen and rook produce the same EHSA class for 100.0% of mainland townships. Agreement with the precision 1-only analysis is 80.1%. The latter changes the reporting subset as well as location certainty, so disagreement cannot be attributed entirely to coordinate error. The main results should therefore be read as patterns in the chosen recorded sample. Areas that remain consistent across specifications provide a firmer basis for follow-up than those whose class changes.

Gi* series have median lag-one autocorrelation 0.71. Temporal neighbourhoods overlap, and ordinary Mann–Kendall assumes independence under its usual null. I therefore shuffle contiguous two-quarter and three-quarter blocks, recomputing the trend score for 999 permutations. The corresponding p < .05 counts are 129 and 114, compared with 165 under ordinary MK. These block tests preserve dependence inside short blocks, but neither guarantee removal of longer dependence nor account fully for seasonality. They are sensitivity evidence, not a universal correction. Bin-level BH classes are also saved in ehsa-results.csv; their adjustment family is all 6,213 mainland quarter bins per specification.

text:
6 Value-added analysis: a spatial scan of redistribution

6.1 Why the extra method adds a different answer
EHSA concerns neighbourhood concentration through time. The spatial scan asks a narrower comparison: where did a larger share of national recorded events move between an early and recent window? I compare January 2021–September 2022 with January 2024–September 2025. Both contain 21 months, with the same calendar-month composition. The intervening period is deliberately omitted from this contrast, while it remains in EHSA.
A Bernoulli spatial scan treats recent events as cases and early events as controls. Circular candidates expand around township interior points, include 1–30 townships, and contain at most 20% of the combined early/recent events. The likelihood ratio compares the recent-event fraction inside a circle with the fraction outside. This conditions on reporting geography rather than using a population denominator. The null randomly reallocates period labels while holding township totals and the national recent-event total fixed. Each of 999 simulations repeats the entire search; the observed statistic is compared with the simulated maximum, accounting for the search over circles. At most three non-overlapping clusters are reported. The R implementation follows the Bernoulli scan likelihood and Monte Carlo logic; it does not run SaTScan software.






Figure 8: Spatial redistribution clusters with search adjusted significance




The strongest selected cluster is centred on Ramree, spans 30 townships, and increases its share from 2.2% to 11.5%. Its recent-to-early share ratio is 5.19, with search-adjusted p = 0.001. This identifies a geographic shift beyond a general national increase. The cluster boundary depends on circular candidates and township representative points; it is not a front line or a forecast. Spatial and temporal dependence between related conflict events may make event-label permutations overconfident, so the scan remains exploratory.







Figure 9: Early and recent national shares for spatial scan clusters




The share comparison makes the scan’s contribution visible. It distinguishes an increase in a cluster’s importance within the national record from an increase that simply follows the countrywide total. The reported groups are non-overlapping, but they do not partition Myanmar and are not ranked aid-allocation recommendations. Differences in reporting access between the two windows could also shift recorded shares.

7 Integrated findings and peacebuilding implications
Accumulated counts, local spatial association and temporal change answer different questions. Monywa has the largest event total but no formal EHSA pattern under the stated rules. Its burden is still substantial. Kawkareik illustrates a significant increasing concentration, while the scan’s leading group around Ramree identifies a shift towards recent events. A single ranking would hide those differences. Reported fatalities add another dimension: they describe estimated severity and can change the priority suggested by event frequency alone.
For humanitarian preparedness, sustained high-burden neighbourhoods support maintaining capacity over time. Significant increasing concentrations suggest locations where field teams could check changing displacement, medical demand and access constraints. High-low outliers call for local verification because a township can stand apart from its immediate surroundings. The analysis does not locate safe travel corridors or justify tactical decisions.
Township labels should start a discussion with local organisations, not settle it. Before reallocating support, combine the statistical evidence with current needs assessments, service capacity, displacement data and operational access. A cold spot may have fewer recorded events because reporting is difficult. Likewise, a diminishing hot spot may still face serious harm despite a declining relative concentration.

title: Myanmar’s changing conflict geography
section: 8 Limitations and what I would improve
text:
8 Limitations and what I would improve

Reporting and measurement: ACLED records reported events and uncertain fatality estimates. Access and source coverage can vary geographically and over time. There is no credible population-risk estimate here.
Location uncertainty: precision 2 makes up a substantial part of the sample. The precision 1 rerun changes which events are represented, not just their spatial accuracy. Eight unmatched points and eight conflicting non-missing township labels warrant source-level checking.
Scale and boundaries: the v9.4 layer is held fixed throughout the period. Township aggregation can conceal local variation and does not represent changing territorial control. Border neighbours outside Myanmar are absent from the spatial comparison.
Statistical reference: permutation tests assume exchangeability. Conflict episodes generate related events; overlapping space-time neighbourhoods induce dependence. BH and short-block checks improve transparency but do not establish independent evidence for every coloured township.
Design sensitivity: the first EHSA quarter lacks a lagged period; 19 quarters offer limited trend resolution. Circular scan candidates can miss irregular corridors. The chosen scan windows and maximum cluster size influence the findings.

The most useful next step is to investigate the locations whose conclusions change with event precision, then add displacement or service-access information with a compatible observation period. This would improve the planning interpretation more than adding another map of the same counts.

9 Reproducing the analysis
Open the repository’s RStudio project. Download the original eLearn ACLED CSV to Take-home_Ex/Take-home_Ex02/data/raw/. The boundary script downloads MIMU v9.4 and checks its content hashes. Install packages recorded in outputs/package-versions.csv, then run:

The seed is 6262026 for local tests, EHSA and block checks, and 6262126 for the scan. The local permutation code uses one core. Scripts check input hashes, row reconciliation, keys, cube balance and finite results. The report reads computed outputs for its numerical claims. The slides consume these same results after the report completes. Raw events, event-level intermediates and boundary geometry stay local. Published material contains original analytical figures and statistical summaries, with source attribution. Input access is required to reproduce the analysis.

9.1 Executable workflow
The preparation code establishes the study window, records the sample exclusions and builds the cube. The analysis code sets the statistical reference and retains each Gi* series. The scan code implements a separate redistribution question. Figure code uses consistent count bands and neutral fills for non-significant areas. # Small transparent helpers, shared by the analysis and its verification.
classify_ehsa02 <- function(gi, p, tau, trend_p, alpha = .05) {
  # Separate bin and trend tests, require the correct sign for each family,
  # and require the final bin for consecutive/sporadic/oscillating classes.
  hot <- gi > 0 & p < alpha
  cold <- gi < 0 & p < alpha
  n <- length(gi)
  classify_family <- function(hit, other, label, direction) {
    proportion <- mean(hit)
    if (!hit[n] && proportion >= .9) return(paste("Historical", label))
    if (proportion >= .9) {
      if (trend_p < alpha && tau * direction > 0) return(paste("Intensifying", label))
      if (trend_p < alpha && tau * direction < 0) return(paste("Diminishing", label))
      return(paste("Persistent", label))
    }
    if (!hit[n]) return(NULL)
    if (sum(hit) == 1L) return(paste("New", label))
    run <- rle(rev(hit))$lengths[1]
    if (run >= 2L && sum(hit) == run) return(paste("Consecutive", label))
    if (any(other)) return(paste("Oscillating", label))
    return(paste("Sporadic", label))
  }
  h <- classify_family(hot, cold, "hot spot", 1)
  if (!is.null(h)) return(h)
  c <- classify_family(cold, hot, "cold spot", -1)
  if (!is.null(c)) return(c)
  "No pattern detected"
}

mk02 <- function(x) {
  r <- Kendall::MannKendall(x)
  c(tau = as.numeric(r$tau), p_value = as.numeric(r$sl))
}

block_trend02 <- function(x, block = 2L, nsim = 999L, seed = 6262026L) {
  # Exploratory sensitivity: shuffle contiguous blocks rather than quarters.
  # This preserves short within-block dependence, not seasonality or all lags.
  n <- length(x)
  blocks <- split(seq_len(n), ceiling(seq_len(n) / block))
  score <- function(z) sum(sign(outer(z, z, "-")[lower.tri(matrix(0, n, n))]))
  observed <- score(x)
  set.seed(seed)
  simulated <- replicate(nsim, score(x[unlist(blocks[sample.int(length(blocks))])]))
  (1 + sum(abs(simulated) >= abs(observed))) / (nsim + 1)
}

title: Myanmar’s changing conflict geography
text:
Research question and study design
Where is recorded armed conflict concentrated, and where is that concentration changing?

53,899 events in 330 Myanmar townships, January 2021–September 2025.
Battles, explosions/remote violence and violence against civilians.
Local Moran’s I and Gi* for spatial patterns. Quarterly Gi* and Mann–Kendall for change.
327 townships in spatial tests. Three islands remain in descriptive counts.


ACLED records reported events. Counts measure recorded burden and concentration.


Sources: ACLED course file, accessed 8 Oct 2026; MIMU township boundaries v9.4. Original sample: 87,109 rows.

title: Myanmar’s changing conflict geography
text:
Monthly frequency and severity


The peak is 1,466 events in November 2023. Event frequency and reported fatalities follow different paths.

title: Myanmar’s changing conflict geography
text:
The recorded burden is uneven




Monywa has the most events: 1,039.
The ten largest township totals account for 15.9% of recorded events.
Kale leads in reported fatalities.
The maps use identical count bands. Neither includes a population denominator.

title: Myanmar’s changing conflict geography
text:
Clusters and spatial outliers




Event counts show 36 high-high townships.
1 low-high outliers have lower counts beside higher-count neighbours.
Global Moran’s I = 0.488, permutation p = 0.001.
Primary colours require two-sided p < .05. Multiple-testing adjustment reduces the number of flags.

title: Myanmar’s changing conflict geography
text:
Gi* identifies concentrated neighbourhoods




39 event hot spots and 51 cold spots at p < .05.
Gi* includes the focal township and its neighbours.
Fatalities reveal a related but different burden pattern.
Low recorded activity needs local verification before any safety interpretation.

title: Myanmar’s changing conflict geography
text:
Emerging patterns over 19 quarters




165 townships have Mann–Kendall p < .05. 150 remain after BH adjustment.
Gi* uses current and previous-quarter neighbours against a fixed space-time reference.
The map filters for significant trends. Persistent classes without a significant trend remain in the report’s results table.

title: Myanmar’s changing conflict geography
text:
The trajectories explain the labels




Cases include the largest burden, the largest increasing final hot spot, and the largest declining concentration.
Filled points have Gi* bin p < .05.
A declining concentration can coexist with a substantial accumulated burden. A class label compresses a more complicated history.

title: Myanmar’s changing conflict geography
text:
Precision and dependence affect confidence


Class agreement: Queen/rook 100%; main/precision 1 only 80.1%. Short-block trend checks give 129 and 114 p < .05 results, versus 165 for ordinary MK.

title: Myanmar’s changing conflict geography
text:
A spatial scan isolates redistribution





The leading cluster around Ramree increases its national share from 2.2% to 11.5%.
Search-adjusted p = 0.001. Equal 21-month windows control duration and calendar-month composition.

title: Myanmar’s changing conflict geography
text:
Peacebuilding implications and limits
Sustained high-burden areas support maintaining humanitarian capacity. Increasing concentrations and spatial outliers suggest where local verification may be useful.
Allocation decisions also need displacement, service capacity and access information. Reporting gaps, uncertain locations and related conflict events limit statistical confidence.
The scan identifies a shift in recorded geography. Its clusters are exploratory and do not define front lines or predict the next incident.

Use the maps to guide questions for local partners and needs assessments.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7: Measuring eldercare accessibility
text:
Where do Singapore’s eldercare centres appear easier to reach from the supplied hexagon origins, and how much does that answer change with the accessibility measure? I follow the data-preparation, Hansen, KD2SFCA and spatial accessibility measure (SAM) sequence in Chapter 17 of R for Geospatial Data Science and Analytics. I then compare their relative rankings and test the five-kilometre catchment choice. This is an exercise in method, not an assessment of whether actual older residents have enough services.
The analysis uses the ZIP supplied for this exercise, not substituted web data. Its four inputs are Master Plan 2014 subzones, a hexagon grid, eldercare centre points and a precomputed network origin–destination (OD) matrix. The workbook describes three inputs as course-prepared teaching data. I therefore keep the raw archive and extracted data local; the site publishes my scripts, summaries and figures, but not the underlying OD records or shapefiles. The reproduction notes and input manifest identify the exact files and checksums.

2 Preparing and checking the data
The archive contains 323 subzones, 3125 hexagon origins, 120 eldercare destinations and 375,000 OD pairs. That is exactly 3125 × 120: every origin has one cost to every destination. The OD file has no missing or duplicated pair, and its total cost equals entry + network + exit cost within a numerical tolerance. Nine subzone geometries were initially invalid and were repaired before the regional join.

The shapefiles already use the SVY21 metre grid, although their .prj metadata omit the EPSG authority code. I assign EPSG:3414 to those existing coordinates; I do not transform them as though they were longitude and latitude. The OD cost is supplied in metres. Dividing by 1,000 makes the distance matrix consistent with the kilometres used by SpatialAcc::ac() and the five-kilometre catchment.


Show R code
subzones <- sf::st_read("Hands-on_Ex/Hands-on_Ex07/data/geospatial/MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL.shp")
hexagons <- sf::st_read("Hands-on_Ex/Hands-on_Ex07/data/geospatial/hexagons.shp")
centres <- sf::st_read("Hands-on_Ex/Hands-on_Ex07/data/geospatial/ELDERCARE.shp")
subzones <- sf::st_make_valid(sf::st_set_crs(subzones, 3414))
hexagons <- sf::st_set_crs(hexagons, 3414)
centres <- sf::st_set_crs(centres, 3414)

od <- readr::read_csv("Hands-on_Ex/Hands-on_Ex07/data/aspatial/OD_Matrix.csv")
wide <- tidyr::pivot_wider(od[, c("origin_id", "destination_id", "total_cost")],
                           names_from = destination_id, values_from = total_cost)
# Align the rows and columns explicitly with the sf feature IDs before modelling.
wide <- wide[match(hexagons$fid, wide$origin_id), ]
distance_km <- as.matrix(wide[, as.character(centres$fid)]) / 1000


The complete preparation script also verifies the archive checksum, every required component, feature IDs, geometry validity and OD arithmetic. The analysis script is the full runnable RStudio workflow. Both expect the repository as the working directory.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7: Measuring eldercare accessibility
text:
3 Hansen potential accessibility
Following the chapter, I give each hexagon demand 100 and each centre capacity 100, then call Hansen potential with a distance-decay power of 0.5. This rewards proximity but allows more distant centres to contribute. The score has no direct interpretation as a count of available places. Its median is 88.7 in this dataset.


Show R code
demand <- rep(100, nrow(hexagons))
capacity <- rep(100, nrow(centres))
hansen <- SpatialAcc::ac(demand, capacity, distance_km,
                         power = 0.5, family = "Hansen")





Hansen potential accessibility at Singapore hexagon origins, with eldercare centres overlaid.


The darker central corridor is expected under a cumulative measure: several nearby destinations contribute to one origin. I joined each hexagon’s representative point to a planning region for a broad comparison. The Central Region’s median Hansen score is 355.2, against 15.8 in the West. This is a spatial description of the supplied centre network and synthetic weights, not evidence that one region’s eldercare needs are met better.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7: Measuring eldercare accessibility
text:
4 KD2SFCA: a bounded catchment
The kernel-density two-step floating catchment area (KD2SFCA) calculation uses a five-kilometre catchment and power 2, as in the workbook. It relates weighted capacity to demand in overlapping service areas. Unlike Hansen potential, an origin with no reachable centre within the threshold receives zero.


Show R code
kd5 <- SpatialAcc::ac(demand, capacity, distance_km,
                      d0 = 5, power = 2, family = "KD2SFCA")





Five-kilometre KD2SFCA accessibility at the hexagon origins.


Here 1,281 of the 3,125 origins have a zero five-kilometre score; the OD matrix confirms that every one of these has no destination within five kilometres. The median KD2SFCA score is only 3.25^{-8}, so the map uses its own legend and I do not compare its numeric values with Hansen scores. A zero is a property of this model catchment, not a proof that residents have no eldercare options.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7: Measuring eldercare accessibility
text:
5 SAM: accounting for competition
The spatial accessibility measure (SAM) uses a power-2 distance decay without the same hard five-kilometre cutoff. It gives a third way to account for the relationship between destination capacity and competing origins. The central tendency is 0.869; the resulting map remains concentrated nearer the existing centres.

                      power = 2, family = "SAM")

7 Catchment sensitivity
I repeated KD2SFCA at ten kilometres to see how sensitive the zero result is to the threshold. Origins with no centre in range fall from 1281 at five kilometres to 639 at ten. The figure partitions all origins by their nearest network distance: 1844 within five kilometres, 642 in the next band, and 639 beyond ten.



Hexagon counts by network distance to the nearest eldercare centre.


The threshold meaningfully changes the apparent coverage. The longest nearest-centre network distance is 32.5 km, although a distance is still not a travel time or a measure of practical access. I would want population by age, actual service capacity, eligibility, mobility and public-transport time before using these surfaces for a planning decision.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7: Measuring eldercare accessibility
text:
8 What I learned
The most useful lesson was that the OD matrix’s ordering matters as much as the formula: a 3,125-by-120 matrix can be dimensionally correct and still connect the wrong origins to centres. Checking every fid before modelling made the workflow more trustworthy. I also learned that a high correlation between two accessibility maps does not make their scores interchangeable. Hansen describes cumulative opportunity, while the five-kilometre KD2SFCA imposes a boundary that leaves many origins at zero. Finally, changing that boundary to ten kilometres showed me how much of the result is an analytical choice rather than a fixed feature of Singapore.
This exercise is limited by the prepared network, its unspecified centre-data vintage, and the identical 100-unit demand and capacity assignments. It cannot establish service adequacy, individual access, or causal effects. The regional summaries are descriptive only; no uncertainty interval or significance test is implied.
